Redman|date=1992 |publisher=WHITBREAD PLC. CHISWELL STREET, LONDON |pages=30 |url=https://www.gla.ac.uk/media/Media_399718_smxx.pdf |access-date=6 October 2024 |quote=The business was known as Whitbread, Martineau & Co. until the mid-1840s.}} is a British [[Multinational corporation|multinational]] [[hotel]] and [[restaurant]] company headquartered in [[Houghton Regis]], England. The business was founded as a [[brewery]] in 1742 by [[Samuel Whitbread (1720–1796)|Samuel Whitbread]] in partnership with Godfrey and Thomas Shewell, with premises in London at the junction of [[Old Street]] and Upper [[Whitecross Street]], along with a brewery in [[Brick Lane]], [[Spitalfields]]. Samuel Whitbread bought out his partners, expanding into [[porter (beer)|porter]] production with the purchase of a brewery in [[Chiswell Street]], and the company had become the largest brewery in the world by the 1780s. Its largest division is currently [[Premier Inn]], which is the largest hotel brand in the UK with over 785 hotels and 72,000 rooms. Until January 2019 it owned [[Costa Coffee]] but sold it to [[The Coca-Cola Company]]. Whitbread's brands include the restaurant chains [[Beefeater (restaurant)|Beefeater]], [[Brewers Fayre]] and Table Table.{{cite web|url=http://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/index.html|title=Our Brands|access-date=3 November 2016|publisher=Whitbread PLC|archive-date=27 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161027053526/http://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/index.html|url-status=dead}} It has not operated a brewery since 2001. Whitbread is listed on the [[London Stock Exchange]] and is a constituent of the [[FTSE 100 Index]]. ==History== [[File:George Garrard, Whitbread Brewery in Chiswell Street (1792).jpg|thumb|Chiswell Street brewery in 1792]] === Origins === The business was formed in 1742 when [[Samuel Whitbread (1720–1796)|Samuel Whitbread]] formed a partnership with Godfrey and Thomas Shewell. They acquired a small brewery at the junction of [[Old Street]] and Upper [[Whitecross Street]], along with a brewery in [[Brick Lane]], [[Spitalfields]], which was used for brewing pale and amber beers.{{cite ODNB|url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/39057?docPos=3|title=Whitbread, Samuel|year=2004 |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/39057 |access-date=31 January 2015}} Godfrey Shewell withdrew from the partnership as Thomas Shewell and Samuel Whitbread bought the large site of the derelict King's Head brewery in [[Chiswell Street]] in 1750.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=14 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} The new brewery was for the specific production of [[porter (beer)|porter]], and was renamed the Hind Brewery after the Whitbread family [[coat of arms]].{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=21 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} While not the first to brew porter, Whitbread was the first to exploit it commercially on a large scale. This coincided with an increase in beer consumption in the UK, following regulations to limit the sale of gin owing to the excesses of the [[Gin Craze]]. By 1758 production at Chiswell street was 65,000 barrels and the firm had become the largest firm of porter brewers in the UK. From the outset, Whitbread was the leading financial partner, and solely responsible for management, and in 1761, Whitbread acquired Shewell's share of the business for £30,000. By the 1780s Whitbread had become the largest brewery in the world.{{cite book|author1=Jack S. Blocker|author2=David M. Fahey|author3=Ian R. Tyrrell|title=Alcohol and Temperance in Modern History: An International Encyclopedia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BuzNzm-x0l8C&pg=PA656|year=2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-833-4|pages=656–657}}{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=11 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} In 1796 the company produced 202,000 barrels of porter. The firm struggled after the death of Samuel Whitbread Sr, and saw ownership transfer to his son, also called [[Samuel Whitbread (1764–1815)|Samuel Whitbread]]. The company adopted the name '''Whitbread & Co. Ltd''' in 1799.{{cite web |url=http://www.whitbread.co.uk/about-us/history-of-whitbread.html |title=History of Whitbread |publisher=Whitbread.co.uk |access-date=2014-04-11 |archive-date=2 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180302102225/http://www.whitbread.co.uk/about-us/history-of-whitbread.html |url-status=dead }} ===Expansion and social welfare=== By the 1810s, Samuel Whitbread Jnr (1764–1815) had brought in several new investment partners including his cousin Jacob Whitbread and the Master Brewer [[Martineau family|John Martineau I]] (1758-1834).{{cite book |last1=Burke |first1=Bernard |title=A Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Landed Gentry of Great Britain...Martineau of Walsham-le-Willows|date=1921 |publisher=Burke Publishing Company |page=1213 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NdQnBjtwLdkC&dq=john+martineau+1834&pg=PA1213 |access-date=5 October 2024 |quote=John Martineau I of Stamford Hill [born 1758] died 1834...}}{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=39 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} Four generations of Martineau's descendants, father-to-son, would later sit on the board of Whitbread, including John Martineau I's great great grandson, [[John Edmund Martineau]]. In 1812, the company merged with the Martineau Brewery holdings and by 1816, leadership was shared between [[William Henry Whitbread]], Joseph Martineau and his father John Martineau I, who died in an industrial accident in a yeast vat in the brewery in 1834. Joseph Martineau became a partner in the business at the time of the merger – the same time as his father John. Three years later, in 1815, annual production reached 161,672 barrels, which at 36 gallons each, equated to over forty-six and a half million pints. Another of John's sons, [[Martineau family|Richard Martineau]], later also became a partner. The business was known as '''Whitbread, Martineau & Co.''' until the mid-1840s. By 1860, William Henry Whitbread - nephew of [[Prime Minister]] [[Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey|Earl Grey]], shared partnership of the firm with John Martineau II (1834-1910) - grandson of John Martineau I and grandson-in-law of [[John Stanley, 1st Baron Stanley of Alderley|Lord Stanley of Alderley]].{{cite journal |title=WHITBREAD AND COMPANY LIMITED {BREWERS} Date(s) 1742-2000 (Creation) |journal=London Metropolitan Archives |date=2000 |url=https://atom.aim25.com/index.php/whitbread-and-company-limited-brewers |access-date=5 October 2024 |publisher=Max Communications Ltd. |quote=William Whitbread (1795-1867), the second son of Samuel Whitbread (1764-1815), and John Martineau became partners in 1860}}{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=57 |isbn= 978-0907383369 }}{{cite book |last1=Deane |first1=Mary |title=The book of Dene, Deane, Adeane. A genealogical history |date=1899 |publisher=Elliot Stock, London |page=139 |url=https://archive.org/details/bookofdenedeanea00dean/page/138/mode/2up?q=Martineau}} In her published 1877 autobiography, John Martineau I's niece, author [[Harriet Martineau]], wrote that she had been a guest at "the great Brewery" in December 1831 where she had presented herself "without notice" to her "kind cousin [John's son, Richard Martineau (1804 - 1865)] and his family" at the "great Brewery [where] night after night, the brewery clock struck twelve, while the pen was still pushing on in my trembling hand". She continued: "I was really glad to be alone during those three eventful weeks, - feeling myself no intruder and being under the care of attentive servants".{{cite book |last1=Martineau |first1=Harriet |editor1-last=Chapman |editor1-first=M.W. |title=Harriet Martineau's Autobiography |date=1877 |publisher=James R. Osgood and Company, Boston |pages=125, 126 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cY0AAAAAYAAJ&dq=night+after+night+harriet+martineau&pg=PA126 |access-date=6 October 2024 |quote=1831, ...}} By 1870, Whitbread had begun producing bottled beers for sale and continued to expand production. On 24 July 1889, the company became a registered limited liability company.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=67 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} In 1914, the firm claimed it was "the largest beer bottler in the world."{{cite book |last1=Turner |first1=David |title=New Developments in the Brewing Industry: The Role of Institutions and Ownership New Developments in the Brewing Industry |date=2020 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780191888854 |page=169 - 191 |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/33760/chapter-abstract/288444749?redirectedFrom=fulltext |access-date=5 October 2024 |quote=Whitbread: "The largest beer bottler in the world”: Developing Whitbread & Co’s Bottling Operation, 1869–1914...In 1914, the London brewer Whitbread & Co. claimed it was the “largest beer bottler in the world.” Arguably it was, it having a network of more than forty bottling depots and stores in Britain and Belgium, with a dozen bottles available anywhere in Britain for 2/6}} By the 1870s, John Martineau II had bought land in [[Eversley]] where he had boarded with his tutor [[Charles Kingsley]]. This was, as reported by the [[Bury Free Press]] in 1902, 'to rebuild cottages and to build fresh ones realising, long before it became the popular cry, that the fundamental basis for improving the health, happiness and morals of England was decent and healthy housing.’{{cite web |last1=Turner |first1=J. |title=Bury Free Press - 6th December 1902 - The Opening Of A New Priory Room 'Another splendid addition to the long list of Mr. John Martineau's gifts to the parishioners of Walsham le Willows |url=https://www.walsham-le-willows.org/clubs-groups-charities/history-group/reviews/number-24-january-2003/ |publisher=Walsham le Willows Parish Council |access-date=5 October 2024 |quote=The Opening Of A New Priory Room ‘Another splendid addition to the long list of Mr. John Martineau’s gifts to the parishioners of Walsham le Willows has just been completed with the erection of a new room for meetings in connection with the church...The Martineau Cottages Next year the Martineau family will celebrate 150 years of residence in and service to Walsham. It was John Martineau (1834–1910) who was responsible for the building of the elaborate estate cottages. Although he inherited the estate on the death of his father Richard in 1865, he did not live here. Instead he maintained the estate for his mother Lucy and his sisters, and visited often. At the age of sixteen John had been sent to Eversley in Hampshire to become a pupil of Charles Kingsley rector there and the author of “The Water Babies”, where he was greatly influenced by and became devoted to him. Later he began buying land in Eversley in order to build cottages there. The Eversley cottages are almost identical to those in Walsham. ‘He bought land in Eversley in order to rebuild cottages and to build fresh ones realizing, long before it became the popular cry, that the fundamental basis for improving the health, happiness and morals of England was decent and healthy housing.’}} ===Guinness Brewery=== From 1904, Whitbread was bottling [[Guinness Brewery|Guinness]] stout.{{cite book |last1=Bone |first1=Robert |title=Research handbook and the history of trademark law |date=2024 |publisher=Edward Elgar Publishing |page=292 |isbn=978-1-78897-310-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RK8pEQAAQBAJ&dq=whitbread+bottled+guinness+beer&pg=PA292 |access-date=3 October 2025}} This cooperation, and rivalry, between the two breweries continued into the 20th century with both firms boasting a [[Masters of the Worshipful Company of Brewers|Master of the Worshipful Company of Brewers]]; [[John Edmund Martineau]], the great great grandson of [[Martineau family|John Martineau]], in 1955 and [[Guinness family|Cecil Edward Guinness]], the great great great great nephew of [[Arthur Guinness]], in 1977.{{cite news |title=Obituary: Edward Guinness obituary Influential director of his family's eponymous brewing company who squared up to the chief executive 'Deadly Ernest' Saunders |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/obituaries/article/edward-guinness-obituary-xkr2jm32d |access-date=3 October 2024 |work=[[The Times]]|date=3 February 2023 |quote=[He was] the great-great-great-great-nephew of Arthur Guinness, who founded the brewery with the eponymous name…Cecil Edward Guinness was born in 1924 in Leyland, Lancashire, the son of Cecil Guinness, the manager of a cotton mill near Chorley, and Betty Knowles Davies...}}{{cite web |title=400 known Masters of the Worshipful Company of Brewers. |url=https://www.brewershall.co.uk/the-company/history-treasures/past-masters |publisher=Brewers' Company |access-date=3 October 2025 |date=2025}} In the 1920s Whitbread introduced the Double Brown which was designed to rival Guinness and was almost a recreation of Whitbread's original [[Porter (beer)|porter]].{{cite journal |title=WHITBREAD AND COMPANY LIMITED {BREWERS} Date(s) 1742-2000 (Creation) |journal=London Metropolitan Archives |date=2000 |url=https://atom.aim25.com/index.php/whitbread-and-company-limited-brewers |access-date=5 October 2025 |publisher=Max Communications Ltd |quote=In the 1920s Whitbread also introduced the Double Brown which was designed to rival Guinness and was almost a recreation of Whitbread's original porter.}} In 2000, ''[[The Guardian]]'' reported that Whitbread was the country's third largest brewer and that Guinness was the largest.{{cite news |last1=Clark |first1=A. |title=Whitbread calls last orders for beer |url=https://www.theguardian.com/money/2000/may/26/personalfinancenews.business2 |access-date=3 October 2024 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=26 May 2000 |quote=Whitbread is the country's third largest brewer. Guinness is the largest.}} === 20th century === [[File:Whitbread 1985-1986.jpg|alt=The 1985–86 Whitbread Round the World Race|thumb|The 1985–86 Whitbread Round the World Race]]By 1905, the Chiswell Street brewery reached its largest extent and annual production throughout the company breweries had reached nearly 700,000 barrels.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=74 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} Production decreased during the [[First World War]] with Whitbread brewing over 575,000 barrels in 1917.{{Cite web|url=http://barclayperkins.blogspot.com/2018/01/kidd-beers-in-early-1917.html|title=Shut up about Barclay Perkins: Kidd beers in early 1917|date=2018-01-04|website=Shut up about Barclay Perkins|access-date=2019-03-01}} In the 1920s and 1930s, the company bought out several other brewers, including the Forest Hill Brewery and its pubs, and later the Kent Brewery Frederick Leney & Sons, with 130 of its pubs. The company was also reorganised under the leadership of Sir Sydney Neville and introduced new ales, including Double Brown ale.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=97 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} Whitbread ended regular production of porter in 1940 due to its declining popularity and a need to rationalise its product range following [[Second World War]] damage to its brewery sites.{{cite web |last1=Pattinson |first1=Ron |title=Let's Brew Wednesday - 1940 Whitbread Porter |url=http://barclayperkins.blogspot.com/2019/10/lets-brew-wednesday-1940-whitbread.html |website=Shut Up About Barclay Perkins |date=30 October 2019 |access-date=30 October 2019}} 565 Whitbread pubs were also extensively damaged in the war, primarily during the [[The Blitz|Blitz]].{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=107 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} The company was first listed on the [[London Stock Exchange]] in 1948 following a decision by the principal owners to take the company public under the direction of WH (Bill) Whitbread.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=110 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} The next three decades saw Whitbreads merged with over a dozen other regional breweries, including Tennant Brothers of Sheffield in 1961 and [[Brickwoods]] in 1971.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=115 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} Between 1961 and 1971, Whitbread's output increased from 46 to 160 million imperial gallons (2.1 to 7.4 million hectolitres) and it became Britain's third-largest brewer by output.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BuzNzm-x0l8C&q=mack&pg=PA657|title=Alcohol and Temperance in Modern History|isbn=9781576078334|access-date=1 February 2015|last1=Blocker|first1=Jack S.|last2=Fahey|first2=David M.|last3=Tyrrell|first3=Ian R.|year=2003|publisher=Bloomsbury Academic }} In 1971, Whitbread inaugurated the [[Whitbread Book Awards]].[http://www.costa.co.uk/media/300231/CBA-Past-Winners-2015-Version.pdf (CBA-Past-Winners-2015-Version.pdf)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150915193952/http://www.costa.co.uk/media/300231/CBA-Past-Winners-2015-Version.pdf |date=15 September 2015 }}. Costa Book Awards. Retrieved 12 September 2015. The next year, Whitbread became the initiating sponsor of the [[Whitbread Round the World Race]], a sailing yacht race [[Circumnavigation|around the world]] held every three years. Whitbread sponsored the race until 2001.{{cite web|url=http://www.yachtingworld.com/features/whitbread-round-the-world-race-59997|title=Drastic early days of broken boats and high drama in Whitbread Round the World Race|publisher=Yachting World|date=12 November 2014|access-date=15 April 2017}} In 1973, the company purchased Long John International, a Scottish distiller whose brands included [[Laphroaig distillery|Laphroaig whisky]] and Plymouth gin.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=130 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} Later spirit acquisitions, also included the distiller James Burrough and the brand [[Beefeater Gin]] which was later sold.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=135 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} Whitbread acquired a 20% stake in [[Television South|TVS]] for £6.5M from European ferries in April 1984.Whitbread buys £6m TVS stake. By Derek Harris Commercial Editor. The Times, Thursday, 12 Apr 1984; pg. 18 By 1982, the company turnover exceeded £1 billion for the first time. In 1984, [[Samuel Whitbread (Lord Lieutenant)|Samuel Charles Whitbread]] became chairman and a reorganisation of the company took place into separate divisions; the spirits arm, including Laphroaig was sold to [[Allied Domecq|Allied Distillers]] in 1989.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=132 |isbn= 978-0907383369}}{{Cite news| issn = 0362-4331| last = Ap| title = COMPANY NEWS; Allied-Lyons Is Buying Whitbread Liquor Unit| work = The New York Times| access-date = 2018-07-21| date = 1989-12-23| url = https://www.nytimes.com/1989/12/23/business/company-news-allied-lyons-is-buying-whitbread-liquor-unit.html}} The company diversified into other hospitality holdings and invested in new ventures in the 1980s and 1990s, including Beefeater, Pizza Hut, Berni Inns, Heineken Steak Bars and TGI Fridays.{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=133 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} In the early 1990s, Whitbread was required to sell almost 2,500 pubs, as a result of the [[Supply of Beer (Tied Estate) Order 1989]] ([[SI 1989]]/2390).{{cite book |last=Ritchie |first=Berry| date=1992 |title= An Uncommon Brewer, the Story of Whitbread |location=London |publisher=James & James |page=137 |isbn= 978-0907383369}} In July 1996, Whitbread purchased the Pelican Group (comprising 110 restaurants under the Dôme, Mamma Amalfi and, primarily, [[Café Rouge]] brands) for £133m,{{cite web|title=Whitbread PLC History|url=http://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/whitbread-plc-history/|publisher=Funding Universe|access-date=26 November 2012}} and in November 1996, Whitbread acquired the restaurant group BrightReasons (owner of brands including [[Bella Pasta]] and [[Pizzaland]]) for £46m.{{cite news |title=BrightReasons Group |url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12030685.brightreasons-group/ |access-date=8 June 2020 |work=Glasgow Herald |date=28 November 1996}} === 21st century === [[File:Whitbread's Stables 1.jpg|thumb|right|The former stables of the Garrett Street Whitbread Brewery in London (erected 1897)]] In 2001, Whitbread decided to sell all its breweries and brewing interests (Whitbread Beer Company) to Interbrew, now known as [[InBev]]. Whitbread-branded alcoholic beverages are still available in the UK, such as canned Whitbread bitter, but these are not produced by InBev, but rather under licence by other producers. InBev controls the use of the Whitbread brand and the hind's head logo for use on beverages. In 2002 Whitbread sold its pub estate, known as the Laurel Pub Company, to [[Ei Group|Enterprise Inns]],{{Cite web|url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4158/is_20020413/ai_n12607979|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080918013012/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4158/is_20020413/ai_n12607979|url-status=dead|archive-date=2008-09-18|title=Enterprise Inns buys 1,860 pubs to become UK's top landlord {{!}} Independent, The (London) {{!}} Find Articles at BNET|date=2008-09-18|access-date=2019-03-01}} and sold its Pelican and BrightReasons restaurant groups for £25m to Tragus Holdings{{Cite news|url=https://www.standard.co.uk/news/whitbread-sells-restaurant-groups-6299454.html|title=Whitbread sells restaurant groups|date=31 May 2002|work=Evening Standard|access-date=31 May 2017|language=en-GB}} (later renamed [[Casual Dining Group]]). The Whitbread & Co brewery building at 52 Chiswell Street in London still survives, although beer ceased to be brewed there in 1976 and it is now a conference and events venue. Still named "The Brewery", it was part of the Earls Court and Olympia Group from 2005 to 2012, when it was subsequently sold to a private investor.[http://business.timesonline.co.uk/tol/business/industry_sectors/consumer_goods/article570406.ece Whitbread sells historic brewery] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612063338/http://business.timesonline.co.uk/tol/business/industry_sectors/consumer_goods/article570406.ece |date=12 June 2011 }} In 2005, it moved its core operations from [[CityPoint]] in central London, to Oakley House in [[Luton]],{{cite web|url=http://www.ukbusinesspark.co.uk/whd92128.htm |title=Whitbread – market intelligence |publisher=Ukbusinesspark.co.uk |access-date=2014-04-11 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222002551/http://www.ukbusinesspark.co.uk/whd92128.htm |archive-date=22 February 2014 }} and then, in 2006, to larger offices at Whitbread Court in [[Dunstable]].{{cite web|url=http://www.businessmk.co.uk/news/art/120/Whitbread-sells-group-headquarters.html|title=Whitbread sells group headquarters|date=1 October 2006|publisher=Business Milton Keynes|access-date=14 April 2017}} In 2006, it went on to sell 239 of its 271 Beefeater and Brewers Fayre sites to [[Mitchells & Butlers]], who rebranded them into [[Harvester (restaurant)|Harvester]], [[Toby Carvery]] and a selection of other brands.{{cite web|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/5202164.stm |title=Business | Beefeater sites bought by M&B |work=BBC News |date=2006-07-21 |access-date=2014-04-11}} In 2013, as part of the [[2013 horse meat scandal]], DNA tests ordered by Whitbread revealed that horsemeat was present in some meat products sold in outlets owned by the company, at the time Britain's biggest hotel group.{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-21468699 |title=BBC News – Horsemeat scandal: Supermarkets 'share anger and outrage' |publisher=Bbc.co.uk |date=2013-02-15 |access-date=2014-04-11}}{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/retailandconsumer/9873300/Compass-and-Whitbread-caught-up-in-horse-meat-scandal.html|title=Compass and Whitbread caught up in horse meat scandal|agency=Reuters|date=15 February 2013|work=Telegraph.co.uk|access-date=1 February 2015}} On 26 February 2013 Whitbread vowed to remedy the unacceptable situation.{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2013/feb/26/whitbread-food-chain-horsemeat-scandal|title=Whitbread makes food pledge after horsemeat scandal|work=The Guardian|date=26 February 2013 |access-date=1 February 2015}} In 2018, Whitbread faced pressure from two of its largest shareholders, hedge fund [[Sachem Head Capital Management|Sachem Head]] and activist group Elliott Advisers, to break itself up by splitting off the Costa Coffee chain, the theory being the individual businesses would be worth up to 40% more than the current market capital value.{{cite web|url=http://www.business-sale.com/news/article/will-costa-coffee-chain-be-up-for-sale-soon-38853.html |title=Business Sale Report – Will Costa Coffee chain be up for sale soon |publisher=business-sale.com |date=2018-04-22 |access-date=2018-04-22}} On 25 April 2018, Whitbread announced its intention to demerge Costa.{{cite web|url=https://www.whitbread.co.uk/media/press-releases/2018/25-04-2018a |title=Whitbread Group Structure Update |publisher=whitbread.co.uk |date=2018-04-25 |access-date=2018-04-25}} On 31 August 2018, it announced that [[The Coca-Cola Company]] had agreed to buy Costa Coffee for £3.9bn.{{cite news |title=Coca-Cola to buy Costa chain for £3.9bn |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-45365893 |access-date=31 August 2018 |agency=BBC News}} In September 2020, the company announced that they would be cutting jobs, warning that 6,000 staff could lose employment. The company blamed the cuts on a slump in hotel guest numbers since the beginning of the UK's [[lockdown]] in response to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom|COVID-19 pandemic]].{{Cite news|date=2020-09-22|title=Whitbread to cut 6,000 jobs as hotel demand slumps|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/health-54246403|access-date=2020-09-22}} [[Samuel Whitbread (businessman, born 1937)|Sir Samuel Whitbread]] died in January 2023 and was the last family chairman of the brewery, who hastened the company’s move from beer to leisure.{{cite news |title=Telegraph Obituaries - Sir Sam Whitbread, last family chairman of the brewer, who hastened the company's move from beer to leisure – obituary |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2023/01/31/sir-samuel-whitbread-obituary-beer-brewing-bedfordshire-hotels/ |access-date=3 October 2024 |publisher=UK Daily Telegraph |date=31 January 2023}} ==Current operations== Whitbread's principal current operations are: [[File:Premier Inn Hotel, Manor Royal, Crawley.JPG|thumb|A Premier Inn in [[Crawley]]]] ===Premier Inn=== {{Main|Premier Inn}} Premier Inn is the UK's largest budget hotel chain, with over 750 hotels.{{cite web|url=http://mobile.bighospitality.co.uk/Venues/Premier-Inn-opens-600th-UK-hotel#.VM17MmisWSo|title=Premier Inn opens 600th UK hotel|access-date=31 January 2015}} In January 2026, it was announced that Whitbread had sold nine Premier Inn hotels to [[LondonMetric Property]] for £89 million as part of a sale and leaseback transaction. Whitbread continued to operate the hotels under new 30-year lease agreements following the sale. The acquisition increased LondonMetric’s Premier Inn portfolio to 22 hotels.{{Cite web |last=Zaidi |first=Afroze |date=2026-01-13 |title=LondonMetric acquires more Premier Inn Hotel sites for £89m {{!}} TheBusinessDesk.com |url=https://www.thebusinessdesk.com/westmidlands/news/2107239-londonmetric-acquires-more-premier-inn-hotel-sites-for-89m |access-date=2026-01-13 |website=West Midlands |language=en}} ===Table Table=== [[File:Table Table signage (Swinging Bridge, Urmston, Greater Manchester).jpg|thumb|Table Table signage (Swinging Bridge, [[Urmston]], [[Greater Manchester]])]] Table Table is a UK restaurant brand. They started as converted Brewers Fayre restaurants. The brand was originally set up in 2006 unnamed; the name Table Table was launched in May 2008. There are around 100 sites in the UK.{{cite web|url=https://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/table-table.html|title=Table Table|access-date=31 January 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206143457/http://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/table-table.html|archive-date=6 February 2015}} ===Beefeater=== {{Main|Beefeater (restaurant)}} Beefeater was launched in 1974. The chain underwent a huge revamp in the early 2000s. It then proceeded to change its name to "Beefeater Grill" for a period but in 2014 reverted to "Beefeater". Beefeater had around 140 restaurants across the UK.{{cite web|url=https://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/beefeater-grill.html|title=Beefeater|access-date=31 January 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150131170428/http://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/beefeater-grill.html|archive-date=31 January 2015}} In April 2024 Whitbread announced plans to sell 126 unprofitable Beefeater and Brewers Fayre restaurants. It also set out plans to close a further 112 restaurants and convert them into more hotel rooms.{{Cite web |last=Anderson |first=James |date=2024-03-11 |title=Whitbread's property team takes the stairway to eleven in FY23/24 |url=https://www.whitbread.co.uk/whitbreads-property-team-takes-the-stairway-to-eleven-in-fy23-24/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=Whitbread PLC |language=en-GB}} Batches of restaurants were sold off over a two year period, with at least 15 (such as Coombe Lodge, [[Croydon]]) being bought by the Papa's Group,{{Cite web|url=https://papasgroup.co.uk/|title=The Papas Group |}} and re-opened as a JD Wetherspoons pubs as part of a franchise agreement in late 2025.{{Cite web|url=https://insidecroydon.com/2025/12/23/coombe-lodge-open-at-last-but-it-doesnt-seem-quite-finished/|title=Coombe Lodge open at last, but it doesn’t seem quite finished|date=23 December 2025|website=Inside Croydon}} In May 2026, Whitbread announced the eventual closure of all 197 of their remaining restaurants (including Beefeater, Brewers Fayre and Bar + Block), with the loss of around 3800 jobs.{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ye5g9m7mpo|title=Premier Inn owner Whitbread to cut 3,800 jobs in savings plan|date=30 April 2026|website=BBC News}} As part of this programme, Mitchells & Butlers acquired a package of seven sites in June 2026. The package included former Beefeater and Brewers Fayre restaurants, which Mitchells & Butlers announced would be converted into Miller & Carter and [[Toby Carvery]] restaurants.{{Cite web |last=Gyton |first=Georgi |last2=MCA |date=2026-06-09 |title=M&B to acquire small package of Whitbread sites |url=https://www.morningadvertiser.co.uk/Article/2026/06/09/mb-to-acquire-small-package-of-whitbread-sites/ |access-date=26 July 2026 |website=MorningAdvertiser.co.uk |language=en}} ===Brewers Fayre=== [[File:Brewer's Fayre, Royal Quay, North Shields - geograph.org.uk - 121055.jpg|thumb|Brewer's Fayre, Royal Quay, [[North Shields]]]] {{Main|Brewers Fayre}} Brewers Fayre is a pub-restaurant brand which was created in 1979. The pubs are designed to look and feel like traditional local pubs but with a particularly strong family presence. There are around 145 pubs across the country.{{cite web|url=https://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/brewers-fayre.html|title=Brewers Fayre|access-date=31 January 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206143435/http://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/brewers-fayre.html|archive-date=6 February 2015}} In April 2024 Whitbread announced plans to sell 126 unprofitable Beefeater and Brewers Fayre restaurants. It also set out plans to close a further 112 restaurants and convert them into more hotel rooms. ===Whitbread Inns=== The Whitbread Inns brand of restaurants was created by Whitbread in 2014. In January 2016 there were 13 pubs (all of which were Table Table) across central and southern England.{{cite web|url=http://whitbreadinns.co.uk/|title=Whitbread Inns|access-date=16 January 2016}} ==Former operations== Whitbread's former operations include: * [[Costa Coffee]], was founded in London in 1971 by the brothers Sergio and Bruno Costa as a wholesale operation supplying roasted coffee to caterers and specialist Italian coffee shops. Acquired by Whitbread in 1995, it had since grown to over 2,861 stores across 30 countries.{{cite web|url=http://www.caterersearch.com/Companies/33934/whitbread-plc.html|title=Catering & Hospitality News|access-date=1 February 2015|archive-date=18 April 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110418151856/http://www.caterersearch.com/Companies/33934/whitbread-plc.html|url-status=dead}} In August 2018, Whitbread announced that it would sell Costa Coffee to [[The Coca-Cola Company]] in a deal worth £3.9bn. The acquisition was completed on 3 January 2019 following a $4.9 billion transaction, with approval from regulatory authorities in the EU and China.{{Cite web|url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20190103005331/en/Coca-Cola-Company-Completes-Acquisition-Costa-Whitbread-PLC|title=The Coca-Cola Company Completes Acquisition of Costa from Whitbread PLC|date=2019-01-03|website=www.businesswire.com|language=en|access-date=2020-01-08}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.beveragedaily.com/Article/2019/01/03/Coca-Cola-completes-Costa-coffee-acquisition|title=Coca-Cola completes Costa acquisition: 'Our vision is to use Costa's platform to expand in the growing coffee category'|last=beveragedaily.com|website=beveragedaily.com|date=3 January 2019 |language=en-GB|access-date=2020-01-08}} * [[Brewers Fayre#Brewsters|Brewsters]], a brand created in 1999. The emphasis was on families and most sites had been built as Brewers Fayre; this was to give Brewers Fayre a more adult feel.{{Cite web|title=Brewster's Restaurants - Break From The Old Routine by Oui 3|website = [[YouTube]]| date=26 March 2009 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MfYCUfB0Exs |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211213/MfYCUfB0Exs |archive-date=2021-12-13 |url-status=live}}{{cbignore}} * [[Taybarns]], an all-you-can-eat American buffet-style restaurant.{{Cite web|url=http://newsvote.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/magazine/8320043.stm|title=Rise of the all-you-can-eat restaurant|website=newsvote.bbc.co.uk|publisher=BBC|access-date=21 June 2016}} There were six sites in England and one (the very first site at [[Swansea]]) in [[Wales]].{{cite web|url=https://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/taybarns.html|title=Taybarns|access-date=31 January 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206143502/http://www.whitbread.co.uk/our-brands/taybarns.html|archive-date=6 February 2015}} * [[Britvic]], a large UK manufacturer of soft drinks, producing brands such as [[J2O]], [[Robinsons (drink)|Robinson's]] and [[Tango (drink)|Tango]] as well as [[Pepsi]] in the UK and Ireland.{{cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/1101148a-5d84-11da-be9c-0000779e2340|title=Britvic IPO to value drinks group at up to £537m|date=25 November 2005|publisher=FT.com|access-date=31 January 2015}} * [[Marriott International|Marriott]] hotels and clubs in the UK, sold to brand owner [[Marriott Corporation]].{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/financetopics/profiles/8081483/When-Alan-Parker-moved-Whitbread-from-beer-to-hotels-no-one-got-it-they-do-now.html|title=When Alan Parker moved Whitbread from beer to hotels no-one got it, they do now|work=The Telegraph|date=23 October 2010|access-date=31 January 2015}} * [[TGI Friday's]] – Whitbread originally held the UK franchise rights to the American restaurant chain [[TGI Friday's]]. The restaurants are known for their "over the top" American style and are popular with teenagers for birthday parties. On 17 January 2007 Whitbread announced that the franchise rights for TGI Friday's were being sold to a joint venture between Carlson Restaurants Worldwide Inc and [[ABN AMRO]] Capital for £70.4m.{{cite web|last=Bill |first=Tom |url=http://www.caterersearch.com/Articles/2007/01/17/310943/whitbread-sells-tgi-fridays-to-joint-venture.html |title=Whitbread sells TGI Friday's to joint venture – Caterer and Hotelkeeper |publisher=Caterersearch.com |date=2007-01-17 |access-date=2014-04-11}} * [[Pizza Hut]] UK, sold to brand owner [[Yum!]]{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2012/nov/09/pizza-hut-restaurants-sold-rutland|title=Pizza Hut restaurants sold to investment group|date=9 November 2012|work=The Guardian|access-date=31 January 2015}} * [[David Lloyd Leisure]] – Whitbread ran more than 50 [[David Lloyd Leisure]] (DLL) clubs in [[Great Britain]] and [[Ireland]], with a further number in Spain, the Netherlands and Belgium. DLL is Britain's biggest tennis operator and manages more than 500 tennis courts. On 4 July 2007, Whitbread announced that it had conditionally agreed to sell the David Lloyd Leisure chain to Versailles Bidco Limited for £925 million. Whitbread will initially use the proceeds from its sale to pay off debt.[http://www.whitbread.co.uk/media.cfm?id=press_releases&view=229 "Sale of David Lloyd Leisure"]. Whitbread plc. 4 June 2007. ''URL accessed 4 June 2007.'' {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070529100311/http://www.whitbread.co.uk/media.cfm?id=press_releases&view=229 |date=29 May 2007 }} * Hogshead, a group of town-centre pubs, similar to Wetherspoons, became part of the [[Laurel Pub Company]] in 2001.{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/4489445/Luminar-eyes-Hogshead-pubs-deal.html|title=Luminar eyes Hogshead pubs deal|date=15 April 2001|work=The Telegraph|access-date=31 January 2015}} * [[First Quench Retailing|Threshers]], a chain of [[off licence]]s.{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/retailandconsumer/6583701/Former-owners-Punch-Taverns-and-Whitbread-face-Threshers-liability.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091119071231/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/retailandconsumer/6583701/Former-owners-Punch-Taverns-and-Whitbread-face-Threshers-liability.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=19 November 2009|title=Former owners Punch Taverns and Whitbread face Threshers liability|date=16 November 2009|work=The Telegraph|access-date=31 January 2015}} * [[Germany]]: Churasco, owned since 1990, and [[Maredo]], owned since 1994; in 1999 the Churasco restaurants had been transformed into Maredo-branded ones; Maredo was sold in 2005.{{cite web|url=http://www.maredo.de/maredo-gruppe/fakten-historie/meilensteine.html |title=Milestones |publisher=Maredo |access-date=31 January 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140419012242/http://www.maredo.de/maredo-gruppe/fakten-historie/meilensteine.html |archive-date=19 April 2014 }} ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==External links== * [https://www.whitbread.co.uk Whitbread official website] * {{PM20|FID=co/024636|TEXT=Documents and clippings about|NAME=}} {{subject bar|auto=y|d=y|Companies}} {{Whitbread}} {{FTSE 100 Index constituents}} {{authority control}} [[Category:Whitbread| ]] [[Category:British brands]] [[Category:Defunct breweries of the United Kingdom]] [[Category:Catering and food service companies of the United Kingdom]] [[Category:Hospitality companies of the United Kingdom]] [[Category:Companies based in Bedfordshire]] [[Category:Companies listed on the London Stock Exchange]] [[Category:British companies established in 1742]] [[Category:Restaurant chains in the United Kingdom]] [[Category:1742 establishments in Great Britain]] [[Category:Food and drink companies established in 1742]] [[Category:Companies in the FTSE 100 Index]]

Whitbread, previously trading as Whitbread, Martineau & Co., is a British multinational hotel and restaurant company headquartered in Houghton Regis, England. The business was founded as a brewery in 1742 by Samuel Whitbread in partnership with Godfrey and Thomas Shewell, with premises in London at the junction of Old Street and Upper Whitecross Street, along with a brewery in Brick Lane, Spitalfields. Samuel Whitbread bought out his partners, expanding into porter production with the purchase of a brewery in Chiswell Street, and the company had become the largest brewery in the world by the 1780s.
Its largest division is currently Premier Inn, which is the largest hotel brand in the UK with over 785 hotels and 72,000 rooms. Until January 2019 it owned Costa Coffee but sold it to The Coca-Cola Company. Whitbread's brands include the restaurant chains Beefeater, Brewers Fayre and Table Table.
It has not operated a brewery since 2001.
Whitbread is listed on the London Stock Exchange and is a constituent of the FTSE 100 Index.
